utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Madam Registrar, could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. The accused are here. Defence teams are in full force. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Nicholls, Mr. Thayer. Yesterday, we ended up still discussing an issue raised by Mr. Haynes by way of objecting to the admission of the witness statement, and we adjourned at that point, after having started discussing it. I wonder if, in anticipation of the beginning of spring, you sat down and came to an agreement. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. Hope springs eternal, Your Honour. I think we have an understanding, if not an agreement. Briefly, I think my learned friend will agree that his assertion that there was some reference in the statement to the effect that none of these 11 prisoners was treated at the Zvornik Hospital was, in fact, an error, and I think the Court will remember well what the actual testimony was there. Nevertheless, my learned friend would argue, I believe, that there are other differences, which we are all familiar with, and I'll just leave it at that. I think that's -- enough has been said as to what the clarifications were, and whether the Court can accept the statement as a 92 ter statement with those clarifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Haynes. If you wish to add anything, I mean it's -- you may have already said what you wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. I've said all I want to say in relation to this witness. I do feel we are reaching a crossroads with 92 terrace as to whether the practices we are currently adopting really are saving us any time at all. I have little doubt that as a viva voce witness, Dr. Novakovic could have been led through in chief in half an hour, and instead we are spending a whole session with him correcting and clarifying, and then we're having to put in a statement of the end bit. But I've said I want to all I want to say in relation to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So we are back to square one, to an extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll be coming to the exhibits to be tendered by the Defence soon. In the meantime, I think we need to -- we've got two documents that have been tendered, and the first is the witness statement which is being contested. This second one is 65 ter number 1884, which I understand has not been objected to by any of the Defence teams, but I put the question again just in case we missed this yesterday. There are no objections to the tendering of -- to the admission of this document, 1884. Just give us a moment to discuss or confer, conclude on 02480, please, and I will be coming back to you in a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I keep it on when I should switch it off, and I have it off when I should have it on. Coming to the question of whether Witness number 156's statement should be admitted or not, and addressing some of the issues that were voiced yesterday, that were raised yesterday, both by Mr. Bourgon and -- and in particular by Mr. Haynes. We'd like to make clear first and foremost one thing, and this is by way of trying to remove any misconception that there might be -- I'm not say that there is, but there might be. Sometimes we do get that feeling about the raison d'etre of Rule 92 ter. When the judges in Plenary decided to introduce Rule 92 ter in addition to the already existing 92 bis, the idea was to streamline procedure by way of economising on proceedings as -- as much as possible without endangering the proper administration of justice, and to supplement what was considered to be a shortcoming in 92 and then 92 bis, which did not cover the whole gamut of testimonies that could be dispensed with in a way that is now being contemplated under the rules. When we introduced Rule 92 ter, the idea was not, and would never be, that once the statement or the evidence of a witness is admitted pursuant to that rule, then that would only be followed by a summary of that statement or testimony with no space available, no -- for either party to, particularly in this case we're talking on the Prosecution of course because this is a Prosecution witness. The idea was never to allow for a situation to obtain where the witness would be brought here, have his statement confirmed as per paragraph 3 of -- subparagraph 3 of paragraph (A), and then have him cross-examined. The idea was that we would be economising on time by introducing the statement pursuant to the rule, accompanied by a summary thereof, and then of course it stands to reason that any questions that may become necessary in order either to supplement or to clarify the contents of that previous evidence or statement would be perfectly in place and would become necessary and were to be allowed. This was the gist of our previous ruling on this matter. It does happen, of course, and it has happened both under 92 bis and under 92 ter, that on reviewing the previous testimony or the previous statement the witness wishes to correct some matter, some parts of that statement; and provided that the previous statement is not replaced by an in -- completely in inconsistent or substantially different, new statement, then this is a procedure that is perfectly -- perfectly normal and is the procedure that was envisaged in the first place when we introduced Rule 92 -- Rule 92 ter. So it is true that in certain instances there hasn't been much saving on time. That is -- that is perfectly true. And our idea on this is that one tries to use one's good judgement with a view to identifying those witnesses which are worth summoning and bringing over to testify under Rule 92 ter and others that would -- can be classified as simply not worth resorting to that procedure to Rule 92 ter at all, and bringing forward those witnesses to testify viva voce. As has been the case, you have changed your mind as you went along, sometimes you asked to convert witnesses from 92 bis to 92 ter, sometimes you have decided to forego that and to bring the witness to testify viva voce, so I'm not saying that you don't use your good judgement. But maybe it should be made use even more, and perhaps better. That having been said, we are not of the opinion that what happened yesterday amounts to a substantive or substantial or material departure from the statement that the witness had made two years, three years prior to coming to give testimony here. We find what happened to be within the parameters of what I stated earlier to be the raison d'etre of Rule 92 ter, and therefore we are ruling for the admission of the witness statement rather than against. All right. So that disposes of this issue. There was another issue that was raised yesterday by more than one party, more than one Defence team in relation to the next witness, 158. We also invited you to make use of the break and any time available after the sitting to try and reach an agreement. If I could refresh your memory, the initial point raised was whether an information sheet amounts to a statement, and then that sort of amalgamated into a fresh argument that seemed to me to supercede the previous one; namely, that now the Prosecution, the Office of the Prosecutor have obtained a proper statement from the witness that has been handed to the Defence teams, and we left it there. I don't think we took the discussion any further. So I would like to have a feedback from Mr. Nicholls on whether there has been progress. We'll do this and then we will come to the Defence exhibits for 156.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe there has been progress, Your Honour. What happened was during the first session yesterday I went out and took a very brief statement from the witness, which has been passed out to you and which was given to the Defence at the first break. In that statement the witness confirms that he read the report, that he made certain corrections, and that other than those corrections the information report accurately reflects everything he said during his interview and that he stated those things, he signed that new statement, which I wish to make part of the 92 ter statement for this witness. It is in essence in this signed statement he incorporates and validates the previous statement. And I believe that there is no longer an objection to proceeding with him on a 92 ter basis, and in this case I believe it will save time and will be quite brief. The corrections and clarifications are already contained in the very short statement I took yesterday, so it should be quite a brief direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. One question, Mr. Nicholls. Do I take that to mean that you will be, for all intents and purposes, dropping 02482 from the list of possible exhibits? That's the information sheet, information report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It would be both the information report and the short statement, which incorporates by reference but not word for word, the information report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you concede also that the information report, once you confirm what you've just stated, as no longer covered by any privilege --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- under Rule 70?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll come to you soon after that, but I just wanted to put my mind at rest that we probably be able to proceed with Witness 158. Now, going back to the previous witness, 156, does any one of the Defence team wish to tender any documents? Mr. Ostojic, I know that Mr. Meek is not here, but...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I checked with Mr. Meek, and we have no documents to tender at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I take it then, there being silence in the courtroom, that there are no documents to be tendered by the Defence teams. So that closes that chapter. Are there any further objections or renewed objections to the commencement of the testimony of Witness number 158? Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, colleagues in the courtroom. Mr. President, I did speak with my colleague yesterday concerning the witness statement that was provided to us yesterday, and we -- again we spoke this morning, and I informed him that I would most likely not address the Court and simply let it go, with a view to trying to take what the Trial Chamber has invited us to do on a number of occasions, which is to take a pragmatic approach to these issues. But in light of what you just said, Mr. President, concerning Rule 92 ter and the way -- what it is intended for, there are issues which I need to bring, and it addresses this specific issue. Yesterday I mentioned to my colleague, Why don't you simply -- the witness is there, make a statement and have him sign, and that's it. We won't -- this has been done in the past for intercept operators where you get a full statement at the last minute. Instead of doing that, my colleague chose to add a statement to confirm the Prosecution's violation of the rule by introducing an information report. Why? It's not for me to say. That's their -- but I simply submit to the Trial Chamber that it would have been much easier simply to do a statement with that witness, and the question would not arise. I mentioned to my colleague yesterday, what we are afraid of is that we say yes for pragmatic reasons the first time and then it goes from the fingers to the elbow to the shoulder, and then the door is fully open. Mr. President, concerning 92 ter, you mentioned a few minutes ago that when the judges adopted this rule, its purpose was to streamline proceedings. What we don't like, I'm speaking for this, the client that I represent in this case, and maybe the others don't join, this is entirely a personal argument but I know that it is shared by others. What we are afraid of with Rule 92 ter is that it is not used by the Prosecution for the purposes that it was intended for. In our view the way the Prosecution is using Rule 92 ter, and when they make a decision to move, either from viva voce to 92 ter or from 92 bis to 92 ter, their purpose is completely different from what it should be. In our view the purpose that the Prosecution is -- the Prosecution's purpose in using 92 ter is to get on the record comments from their investigators, which are included sometimes in statements, sometimes in information reports. It is to use the opportunity to have both. They want the cake and they want to eat it, too. They want the written piece of evidence and then they want the opportunity to be able to cross-examine their own witness with respect to the contents of the material that is "put on the record." As my colleague put to you a few minutes ago, it is not using -- saving any time, and it is also prejudicial to the accused because they actually use the statement to then in the guise of clarifying to lead the witness and to cross-examine their own witness on the stand. We don't save time. It is prejudicial to the accused, and it seems the Trial Chamber is not seeing what the Prosecution is doing with these statements. That's our argument today, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey. I think we can close the discussion here. Please, let's proceed with -- with the next witness. What I can say would be very short; namely, there is a pending motion regarding three witnesses, three remaining witnesses out of 12 that the Defence teams contest by way of maintaining that they should not be produced or allow the Prosecution to produce them pursuant to 92 ter. We will decide that matter. We don't automatically grant every motion or every request made by the Prosecution for resorting to Rule 92 ter. And as I said earlier, we enjoin the Prosecution for the time being because it's the Prosecution to use its -- or use the best judgement possible in identifying those -- those cases. I don't think we are with you, Mr. Bourgon, that we haven't saved time or we haven't streamlined the proceedings. It is only in just a handful, less than a handful of instances that perhaps the time saved was -- was very little. But we still saved time, I must say. So let's -- yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa used two documents in cross-examination. The first, which we would ask to be tendered into evidence, is 7D169 which is a page from the duty officer's notebook of the Zvornik Brigade of the 6th of July. The second was 3D17 which was the list of -- which was the Red Cross list of prisoners. And we believe that was admitted under that title, 3D17, on the 7th of November, so we don't ask that to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Registrar can check that immediately. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We have no objection obviously to the notebook. That is a document we would prefer to be admitted in whole, and we will seek to do at a later time in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for the record, it's -- it reads the 6th of July. It was the 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We'll check that and if it's not -- it's correct, I'm told. It's correct. Thank you. So the first of these documents is admitted, the other has been admitted already. No further documents? All right. No further exhibits. Witness 158.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, yesterday you mentioned his age. Can we anticipate or should we anticipate any problems or any special breaks?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't think so, Your Honour, but I've told the witness if he begins to feel tired that he -- that there is no problem, he should just let us know. But I think -- I don't -- I don't want to speak for the Defence, but I don't think this whole process is going to take very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. The Defence have indicated two hours. Incidentally, Ms. Condon, we haven't yet had time to discuss the matter raised by you yesterday, and that's the reason why we haven't come back to you as yet. But we will, at the earliest opportunity. We have other matters, too, that we are dealing with, some of which are urgent.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dr. Gavric, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, you are required to make a solemn declaration here, equivalent to an oath, that you will be testifying the truth. That is the text of the solemn declaration. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your commitment with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Dr. Gavric. Please take a seat, make yourself comfortable. I am very optimistic that your testimony will begin and finish today. Before I hand you over to Mr. Nicholls, I just wanted to tell you one thing. If at any time you need a break or you are feeling tired and you wish us to stop for a short while, then please don't hesitate to tell us and we will have a break immediately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The procedure here is Mr. Nicholls will go first, and then he will be followed by some of the Defence teams on cross-examination. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry you waited for some time yesterday, and we'll try to be quite quick with your testimony today. First of all your full name is Jugoslav Gavric; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you tell us when you were born, please?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of May, 1933.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you just a couple questions now about the interview you gave to investigators in 2003 and also the statement which you signed in my office yesterday. Now, first of all, in my office earlier this week did you read the report of your 19th of January, 2003, ICTY interview in your own language? Do you remember doing that?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And yesterday, in the morning, do you remember signing a brief statement in which you formalised and stated that you had reviewed the report of your earlier interview and in which you wrote down some corrections to that earlier interview? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, other than those five corrections you made, which are in the statement, can you attest that the report of your ICTY interview and the witness statement you signed yesterday morning, both accurately reflect what you stated?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you also confirm that your answers would be the same if you were asked the same questions today here in court?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll now read a brief summary, and so this is not a question for you. In July 1995 Dr. Gavric was Director of the Zvornik Medical Centre. At this time the Chief Medical Officer of the VRS was Dr. Ratko Rokvic, who was based at the HQ in Han Pijesak. Dr. Rokvic was a schoolmate, had been a schoolmate of Dr. Gavric, and they still knew each other in 1995 and would sometimes speak on the telephone. During the period from 11 to 15 July, 1995, there were no Muslims hospitalised in the Zvornik Hospital, then Dr. Gavric received an order from Dr. Rokvic. The order was to go to the Milici Hospital and have the wounded Muslim patients there transferred to the Zvornik Hospital. And Dr. Gavric cannot recall for sure whether this was a verbal or a written order. Dr. Gavric went to the Milici Hospital with a nurse. The driver of the vehicle was a person in uniform, a military uniform, and a police officer was also present on this trip. There were between ten and 15 wounded Muslim men at the Milici Hospital. Three or four of whom were heavily or severely wounded. The names of these patients were contained on a list which was given to Dr. Gavric. Dr. Gavric introduced himself to the patients at Milici Hospital and they -- because they seemed to be afraid. All of these Muslim patients were then transferred to Zvornik Hospital, and each patient carried a copy of his medical records with him. Unfortunately, the vehicle ran out of fuel on the way from Milici to Zvornik, which caused a delay. When he arrived at Zvornik, Dr. Gavric transferred the patients into the care of Dr. Zoran Lazarevic. At this time some civilians and some patients began to protest and were upset about the admission of Muslim patients into the Zvornik Hospital. Dr. Gavric, after he transferred the patients into the care of Dr. Lazarevic, never saw these patients again and he later heard that they were taken away during the night to Tuzla. That concludes the summary. Dr. Gavric, I have just a few questions for you. First, was that summary correct, of what you have stated in your previous statements?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. My first question is, if could you tell us to the best of your recollection what date it was when you went to pick up the Muslim patients from Milici to bring them to the Zvornik Hospital?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: Right now I can't remember the exact date or, rather, day of the week. And as for the date, it was mid-June. I can't remember either the day or the date. I assume, however, it was during the week, not on the weekend, but I'm not fully certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to be clear, are you speaking of June or July?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: July, July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, what kind of vehicle was it that you took to transport these wounded Muslim patients?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: The information that I received that a group of patients needed to be transferred from the Milici Hospital to our hospital in Zvornik indicated that they were patients who couldn't walk on their own. As a result, we found a bus that had been adjusted to transport patients who were lying. Thus, one could place stretchers with patients on them, with the wounded on them, into that bus and transport them in that way. And in addition to that, there were also seats for those who could sit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you just tell me approximately how long the journey from Milici to Zvornik lasted? If you can tell us when you left Milici and when you arrived at Zvornik with the patients?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: We arrived in Milici sometime around noon; 12.00 or 1.00. It took us some time to take over the patients, that lasted for perhaps an hour. I spoke to some people there, some of the colleagues, informed myself about what was going on. I was told that all of the wounded had been treated, medically treated, that they were all receiving therapy, medical therapy, and that each of them carried their own medical history. As far as I can remember, I only carried the list of the wounded with their names and no other information. And this could have lasted for about an hour, that entire procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And when did you arrive back in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, we set out from Milici. It was a warm, sunny day. Then halfway to Zvornik we ran out of fuel. Our bus ran out of fuel. So we had to stay there and wait for somebody to come with the fuel. However, since during that period of time the traffic between Milici and Zvornik was basically non-existent, and we couldn't expect anyone to bring fuel on foot to us, we managed to get some fuel from a nearby inn. We could have lost an hour there on the road, and we arrived in Zvornik towards the evening. I don't remember exactly the time, but it was before the sun set. So this trip, due to these circumstances, was -- lasted longer than normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And after -- after transferring the patients to the care of Dr. Lazarevic, did you ever ask about what had happened to the patients or where they had gone? Did you ever ask anybody that?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, since I completed that task, and it was after business hours at that point, I typically didn't have to do night shifts. I normally spent nights in my apartment. The next day, when I arrived at work, I inquired whether all of the wounded were alive, because, based on what I could see among them, there were several seriously ill patients. I was told that all of them survived that night and that they were evacuated to Tuzla in order to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you now -- a different topic, if you can answer briefly. Do you recall whether there were -- during the war, were there ever any Muslim children treated in the Zvornik Hospital?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: I remember that at the paediatric ward we had a boy who was between seven and nine years old. This boy was hospitalised at the paediatric ward for a longer period of time, a couple of months, if I remember correctly. During that period of time we attempted to find a way to reunite the boy with his family. I think we attempted to do that through the International Red Cross. But we didn't manage, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think this is my last question, probably. But to the best of your memory, it was a long time ago, what time period was it that that little boy you have just described was in the paediatric ward?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: I assumed office there in June of 1993. And I think that already back then I knew that there was this boy at the paediatric ward. I think that that's how it was. As for how long he stayed there, I wouldn't be able to tell you. I don't know until what time he remained and what happened to him afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls. I have on my list all the Defence teams with the exception of the Borovcanin Defence team. Who is going to go first? Mr. Zivanovic. You requested 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Gavric. I'm Zoran Zivanovic, and I'm defending Vujadin Popovic in these proceedings. Could you clarify something for me. If I understood you well, the patients who were brought from the Milici Hospital to the Zvornik Hospital remained there just overnight. Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: I don't know how long exactly they remained. But on the following day, when I came to work, when I came to my office, I think that that was the first thing I inquired about. My assistant told me that all of them were fine, that they had survived that night, and that they were evacuated and were no longer there. That was on the very next morning. That's at least as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next thing I wanted to ask you is whether you knew whether their names were entered into the records of the Zvornik Hospital?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: When I arrived with them, with the wounded, when they were carried into the hospital, those who were on the stretchers, when they were taken to the surgical ward, at the very entrance into the hospital, in the corridor, I gave the list with their names to one of the colleagues who I thought would take over them from me. But then I did not inquire afterwards whether these patients were recorded in the logbook, registration book of patients and so on. Because it wasn't really my duty. At least I didn't consider it to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So after the following morning, when you were told that all of them were fine and they had gone to be exchanged, you never received any information from your staff about the further fate of these people?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: No, nobody informed me of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said, among other things, that at the time when these civilians, patients -- or, rather, when these patients were brought in from Milici, some civilians and some patients started protesting due to the fact that you had admitted some Muslim patients into the hospital. So could you please explain what kind of a protest it was? What was it about?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: See here, Zvornik is a small town and the hospital is in the very centre of the town. Naturally, as the bus passed through the town and when we stopped in front of the entrance into the hospital, the residents were able to see what was happening and they approached us. I could see them approaching, probably thinking that those were the wounded soldiers of the army of Republika Srpska. They could see the stretchers, patients who were unable to walk and so on. So a group of people assembled, a group of eye-witnesses who saw all that. So I had to ask for some security to come. When they learned that these people were Muslims, then their protest became rather firm. We had a problem. We had to ensure that these wounded were kept separately from other wounded at the hospital. It was a problem, however the head of that ward took care of that. I am not sure exactly where these people were accommodated in the hospital itself in the surgical ward. I don't know whether they had enough beds for them there or they perhaps had to be moved to the gynaecology ward, because they had a lot of beds as well. And if there wasn't sufficient room sometimes they used the other ward as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Who is going next? Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have no questions for this doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor. I only have a few questions for you this morning. My first question relates to the -- the reason for which these prisoners were taken from Milici to the Zvornik Hospital. And can you confirm that the reason that they were indeed transferred was because of the small capacity of the Milici Hospital, the fact that there was not enough staff there, and that Zvornik was the closest place to the exchange. Can you confirm this information?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, it was a typical routine. Since the Milici Hospital was significantly smaller, if they could not care for some patients, wounded, then the Zvornik Hospital would typically take them over because we were much larger, when it came to admitting the wounded and the sick. It was my understanding that that was the only reason, because they, in Milici, could no longer care for these people and that they had no room for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I would just like a quick question concerning the moment where your vehicle ran out of fuel. My understanding is that when this happened there was a drinking fountain close to that vehicle and at that point the atmosphere was quite relaxed and actually the people who were wounded on the bus were let out to drink water and come back on the bus. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, since we waited somewhat longer, there was a fountain there, a source of water. It was a warm day and some of the wounded came out, refreshed themselves, cooled down, had some water and then went back to the bus. There were no problems there. There were no discussions, nothing. We simply stood there waiting. And people had some water.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Now, my next question relates to the -- what you discussed a bit with my colleague representing another of the accused in this case, concerning the fact that when you arrived some people gathered because of the arrival of the wounded Muslims. Now, my question is very -- very simple. For you, as a doctor, whether a patient is a Muslim, a Serb or a Croat would make no difference and they would all be treated the same, and indeed, this is what happened to these wounded Muslim prisoners. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Even the clothing that the wounded wore, they were just hospital pyjamas. So even in that sense there was no difference amongst the patients. The treatment was the same. I don't know what else I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. My next question relates to the question which was posed to you concerning the Muslim boy that was held in the paediatric ward for some time. Now, you were the director of the Zvornik Hospital and I would like to know, to the best of your recollection, whether any problems arose from the fact that a Muslim boy was cared for at the Zvornik Hospital or whether any such problems were brought to your attention by anyone working at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: The boy was at the paediatric ward. He was already a bit older than the rest of the patients. I personally went to visit him. And the atmosphere at the ward was quite proper. He even entertained the rest of the patients on the ward, the other children. And I didn't notice any kind of intolerance or even the doctors who were treating him, they had accepted him as a kind of favourite. A boy who, due to circumstances, was there. I didn't notice that he was suffering from any illness. And all of us, the paediatricians and I, remember that we tried to get the International Red Cross to find a way for the boy to find his family. I think I had information that some relatives of the boy were in Germany, and that there were attempts to do it that way. But I don't know what the actual outcome was of that whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Doctor. I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon. I have -- who wishes to go next? Mr. Josse or Mr. Krgovic for General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Gavric.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In your answers to the Prosecutor's questions, you mentioned that the order or information that you needed to go to Milici, you received from the medical corps chief of the VRS, Mr. Rokvic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the order or the piece of paper instructing me to go. But now I assume that -- and I assume that when I gave the statement also, that that was the usual practice regarding the military or the wounded. Then I would get in touch with the -- my colleague, Mr. Rokvic, and also Dr. Davidovic in Milici. I think that he also told me that this was an order -- yes, an order to do that. I repeat once again, I'm sorry, but I cannot remember whether it was a written information or it was information given over the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. So the only person that you were in contact with from the Main Staff regarding the evacuation and regarding any medical issues that had to do with the wounded was actually Dr. Rokvic?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: He was a colonel by rank; is that correct? A primarijus?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown document 0501888. I think that there is an English version and a B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P01888.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm going to show you a note signed by the director of the Milici Hospital. It's going to appear on the screen in front of you shortly and I would like to ask you to confirm whether that corresponds to what you referred to in your answer. It states there that, according to the orders of the medical corps chief of the VRS, the chief of the municipality and the chief of the public Security Service of Milici, the wounded are being transferred to the Zvornik Hospital?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that on the basis of this I organised the transport, I took over the wounded. It was important to me that this was ordered by the chief of the medical service, but I don't remember the part about the chief of the public security service in Milici. What was relevant for me was the information itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll down please, so that we can see the signature on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then you will see.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my glasses are not the best. Yes, yes, I see that this is Dr. Davidovic. He is head of the -- or the director of the hospital in Milici. And this was based on the above order, so...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Krgovic. I have on the list remaining the Miletic and the Pandurevic Defence teams. Madam Fauveau for General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We won't have any questions for this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau. And Mr. Haynes or Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Yes, just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Dr. Gavric. Earlier you said that it was the procedure that patients from the Milici Hospital, which was smaller, if there was no room, they would come to the Zvornik Hospital which was bigger. Can you tell us, if you remember, that day when you came to collect the wounded to bring them from Milici to Zvornik, do you remember if the Milici Hospital was full?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: I didn't have the opportunity, and I didn't really pay attention to the actual part where the patients were. I just came to the director's office, that was Dr. Davidovic. I don't remember seeing him actually on that occasion, but one of the colleagues gave me the list. I don't recall meeting Dr. Davidovic at that time. But I know, from previous visits, that the hospital didn't have many rooms and beds to accommodate surgery patients. And it was logical to me, in a way, for those 15 wounded to be admitted to a larger facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you. In your view, and because you have many years of experience in the medical profession, would you agree with the claim that arises from what you yourself have said, that is that their condition was the reason why they were being transferred to a larger hospital?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: When they came to the Zvornik Hospital you said, when they were being brought out from the buses that came from Milici to Zvornik, that people were interested who was in the buses and that there were certain protests. You also mentioned that the surgical ward was full and that they were put on the -- accommodated at the gynaecology ward which is not really so great. Would you agree that the reason why they were transported from the Zvornik Hospital to the Standard medical facility was precisely that reason, as well as this was done for their personal safety reasons?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: I think both reasons could be valid. At the infirmary, there were certain capacities for a certain number of patients. There was a certain number of beds. And I know that certain wounded persons were treated there at the infirmary. But I didn't get information that they were transferred to the infirmary. I didn't get that information. I was told that they had been evacuated and, from what I can recall, I was not told that they were transferred to the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: And do you believe that their personal safety would be better guaranteed at the infirmary rather than at the hospital in view of the situation that was there?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, because of the situation, yes. Although your remark that the gynaecological ward was not -- we had more than 10 beds there that were empty in the gynaecological ward at the time. And the conditions there for treatment are very good. I believe that, for security reasons, this was a much better move.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: This has been confirmed to a degree, but we would like to know that for certain. And so could you please tell us, the people, that part of the wounded who were taken from the hospital to the Zvornik Brigade infirmary that was close by, did they receive, in your opinion, in your knowledge, and according to the adequate treatment that was available there, did they receive adequate medical care?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: We tried in any case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you. The witness has just stated that he wasn't told that they were taken to the infirmary. He was just told that they were evacuated and he doesn't know that they were taken to the infirmary. So I don't think the question is proper, putting to the witness now that you've told us that they were taken to the infirmary, how were they treated there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let me confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Problem as Mr. Nicholls sees it, and I'm waiting for feedback from my colleagues is that if you look at line 2 on page 27, and line 3, the witness in reply to a previous question said, "But I didn't get information that they were transferred to the infirmary." The objection now is, or the point raised now is that you are putting to the witness, as a fact, that these wounded persons were taken from the hospital to the Zvornik Brigade infirmary. And that is being object --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And also, sorry, that the specific question is, did they receive adequate medical care at the -- which he -- he has said he doesn't have a basis for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So perhaps you can either drop the question or rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My intention was to ask Dr. Gavric, in view of the fact that they were taken away, he doesn't know, this is in -- beyond dispute. And in the previous answer he said that they could receive adequate medical protection at the ambulatory facility. So specifically referring to these wounded, if they were taken, and they were taken there, we know that, it's a fact they were taken there, could they have received proper medical treatment. I'm not asking for his confirmation that they were taken there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, the question is being rephrased. It's being put to you, Dr. Gavric, if these persons were indeed transferred to the infirmary, would -- would it have been likely or possible for them to receive proper treatment in that infirmary? And that's if you know, I mean, if you're familiar with the infirmary and the kind of treatment that could be provided there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the infirmary it was possible to treat and to administer therapy for those patients who had been previously surgically treated before. It was not possible to conduct surgeries or any kind of more serious treatment at the infirmary, but it was possible to continue therapy that was started before. The equipment was fairly good and the staff should have been at the appropriate level. When I am talking about -- I'm talking about doctors, specialists. Again, I would like to repeat, it was not possible for them to receive more complicated treatment, but to continue treatment, it was possible, that was the purpose of the infirmary. It was meant for those who had already been primarily treated to receive further or additional treatment there at the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: And my next question: Dr. Gavric, do you know if specialists and nurses from your institution went to the Standard infirmary to give medical assistance there to the wounded, injured, to the sick at the infirmary?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Do you know about other cases, other than these wounded that we were talking about, if any other Muslim wounded persons were brought to your hospital to receive medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: I really cannot be sure about that, but we were very busy at the time, and all those who came received treatment, so I couldn't really say what numbers we're talking about when and so on, but all wounded that happened to find themselves in our region received treatment there and, from what I can recall, there were no objections or any problems in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: And was the treatment the same, regardless of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was the same. I state that because I gave treatment myself the whole time and I never differentiated on the basis of things like that when patients were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: And was this true both of civilians and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps the wounded had priority in relation to civilians, and of course triage was made, which in those conditions of war is absolutely essential. But there was no difference made as far as treatment was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sarapa. That brings to an end the cross-examination. Is there re-examination, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have no further questions for you, Doctor, which means that, as I anticipated earlier on, your testimony ends here. You're free to go back home. Our staff will assist you. But before you leave this courtroom, I would like to, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, thank you for having come over to give testimony, and also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exhibits. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just P02482 and P02482B, which is the 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections? I hear no objections. So these are -- two documents are admitted. Exhibits from the Defence teams. I understand that the Gvero Defence team would like to tender a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We would, Your Honour. The one that Mr. Krgovic put to the witness, which I think is 6DP01888.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's correct. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So this document, what is -- exhibit is also admitted. And I think we can close this chapter and move to the next witness. Again, I just want to check that there are no protective measures in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's being suggested that we have the break now. I think that's fit and proper. We'll have 25 minutes' break now and we'll start with the new witness afterwards. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Dr. Begovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, you are required by our Rules to make a solemn declaration that you will testify the truth. The text is being handed to you now. Please stand up, read it out aloud, and that will be your commitment with us that you will be testifying the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. Doctor, Mr. Vanderpuye will go first for the Prosecution, and he will then be followed by some of the Defence teams on cross-examination. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a 92 ter witness, so I intend to follow the procedure set forth in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Doctor, do you recall having given a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor which you signed and acknowledged on the 2nd of April, 2003?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was the statement that you gave at that time a truthful statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: The statement was truthful, but two days ago I had some corrections to make because it wasn't fully consistent with what I stated three years ago. At the time, when the gentleman interviewed me, since the statement was in English and not in Serbian, it was read out to me and I did have certain corrections then to make, and then two days ago when the statement was read out to me, I could see that it wasn't written down exactly as I had stated things three years ago. Thus, I had some corrections to make, and two days ago, we clarified that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, before you continue, perhaps you can ask him for his name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Oh, okay. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for the record, except that I addressed him as Dr. Begovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just for the record, could you please state your first and last name?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Zoran Begovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we were just talking about some of the corrections that you made with respect to the statement, but before we get --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- but before we get to that, let me just ask you, when you read your statement recently, before testifying here today, did you read that in your own language?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have it read back to you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: The lady who was an interpreter in 2003 read it out to me in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Just recently, a couple of days ago, did you have an opportunity to read the statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: No. I read it for the first time two days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And when you read the statement two days ago, did you read it in your own language?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And after having read the statement in your own language, did you bring these corrections that you have just spoken about to my attention?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, with respect to those corrections, I'd just like to clarify what they are for the record. With respect to paragraph 8 where it -- and that's for the benefit of the Court, where it says, or indicates that a Major Obrenovic told you that the exchange of the wounded people was pursuant to an order of the Main Staff and General Mladic, would it be accurate to say that Major Obrenovic never actually mentioned that it was -- that the exchange was pursuant to an order of the Main Staff or General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, the day before the order arrived, Mr. Obrenovic addressed me at the infirmary where other members of the medical corps were. He addressed me with the following words: He said, "The wounded arrived. They will stay here for a couple of days until they are exchanged in Bijeljina. Until that time, they should come to no harm. You must take very good care of them. A surgeon will come from Zvornik specifically to treat them."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could stop you there. I just want to focus on this statement. We'll get to the substance of what he told you a little bit later, but did he mention an order or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: No. The order did not arrive until the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to paragraph 9, where it says in effect that you were informed by a nurse that the wounded had been taken away at 5.00 a.m. Would it be more accurate to say that you weren't informed by any particular nurse, but you were informed by a number of people who were aware of the circumstances concerning those wounded?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And would it also be fair to say that the conclusion that they were taken away at around 5.00 a.m., that's contained in that paragraph, was not something that was actually told to you, but something that you yourself surmised?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. The gentleman asked me, since I arrived at around 6.00 at the barracks, the gentleman asked me what was my opinion about when that could have happened. And I said, in my opinion, it could have been between 4.00 and 5.00. But that's just my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to paragraph 11 in the statement, where it says that you received the information from the nurse about the prisoners, and that they were taken away without medical supervision. Is that basically the same correction that you weren't -- you didn't receive that information from any particular nurse? Would that be a more accurate reflection of what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't a nurse who told me that they had been taken away at 5.00, because it was said at 6.00 when some preparations were made, and among others, there were also nurses there. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that the reference in paragraph 11 to the wounded being taken away without medical supervision, would it be more accurate to say that, as far as you were aware, they were taken away without any medical personnel, technicians or doctors, from the place where you worked?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. None of the medical staff escorted them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And finally, with respect to paragraph 13, where the statement indicates that you do not remember Colonel Pandurevic coming to the medical centre in relation to the wounded people, would it be more accurate to say that you do remember that, in fact, he did not come to the medical centre in relation to those wounded people?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pandurevic, at the time, and I said this three years ago, and I will repeat it now. At the time, Mr. Pandurevic was not present in the barracks at all. I saw Mr. Pandurevic for the first time after all of these events, after they ended and when they passed through to Boljkovac. So Mr. Pandurevic was not able to visit them because he wasn't present there. At the time, Mr. Dragan Obrenovic substituted in for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, other than these factual inaccuracies that we have just gone through, which are a fair number, does the statement otherwise accurately and -- does it accurately reflect what you said when you were questioned in 2003, and does it accurately and fairly reflect what you would say, were you to be examined here today?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: You know what, in item number 1, where it says that I volunteered to give information, that's not correct. I received notice, a policeman came to the infirmary and gave me a notice to appear on the following day at 3.00 to meet with the OTP investigators. So that was a correction I wanted to make, and the gentleman didn't respond to it. And then there were other things that didn't -- that weren't included into the statement. It wasn't just those wounded, but after those wounded, there was another group of four or five wounded who were treated and they went to be exchanged in Bijeljina very soon thereafter. However, that wasn't included in the statement, and I made that correction back in Zvornik when the statement was read out it me. However, it was never included in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. But as far as what's reflected in the actual statement, other than what we've spoken about, is the statement accurate?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: As it stands now, yes, and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. With the court's permission, I would tender the statement, subject to the corrections as appear on the record. P02481 into evidence pursuant to 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We'll come to that formally at a later stage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have a very brief summary, although it seems as though you have already heard it. The witness was born in Sekovici in 1964 and in 1992 he began working as a physician at Zvornik Hospital. Shortly after commencing work at the hospital, the witness was transferred to Kozluk medical centre where he remained until his mobilisation to the VRS in mid-1994. On the day of his mobilisation, the witness reported to the medical centre of the Zvornik Brigade at Standard in Zvornik. As chief of the medical centre, the witness was responsible for the provision to Zvornik Brigade soldiers of medical services and reported to the officer in charge of rear services which at some point became Captain Sreten Milosevic. The director of the hospital was Jugoslav Gavric. In July 1995, without any prior notification to the medical centre, approximately 10 to 15 wounded prisoners arrived at the Standard barracks from Zvornik Hospital. The prisoners had received some apparent treatment prior to their arrival and were registered with the medical centre after their arrival. Either the day the prisoners arrived or the following day, Major Obrenovic informed a number of the medical team that they were, that is the -- the wounded were to be transferred to Bijeljina. The witness read a fax to this effect the next day which further called for the prisoners to be given "special care" because they were to be exchanged. Throughout the prisoners' stay, a different physician from Zvornik Hospital came to the Zvornik Brigade medical centre to change their bandages. About five days after their arrival, the witness was informed that the prisoners had been removed from the Standard. An MP later confirmed that they had been taken away by bus. Though the witness did not know what happened to the prisoners, he made no official complaint, believing that their removal had been for the purposes of which he had been previously informed. That concludes my 92 ter statement and I would like to put to the witness a few questions if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Go ahead. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just have one question that I -- at this point in time, because we have a summary that is being read out, and it appears to me that there are some differences between the summary and the corrections that were just brought by the witness to his statement. I note in particular -- I'm trying to stop the page here, on page 38 at lines 16 to 18, the summary read by my colleagues says, "In July 1995, without any prior notification to the medical centre, some people arrived at Standard barracks from Zvornik Hospital." Now -- when the witness was reading -- was making corrections to his statement, and I'm looking here, I'm looking at page 35, lines 6 and subsequent lines. First of all, the day before the order arrived, Mr. Obrenovic addressed me at the infirmary where other members of the medical corps were. He addressed me with the following words: "The wounded arrived. They will stay here for a couple of days". So I understand from this that there was some kind of prior warning by Major Obrenovic and the summary doesn't say that. I would just like to get some clarification either from the witness or from my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think I can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can do that, but on the other hand, also, the witness said that -- I leave it in your hands. But I think it needs some clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think the following will perhaps satisfy my colleague, is that the witness had indicated that Major Obrenovic came before the order and the order was a faxed order which is what is indicated in the statement itself. And the statement itself, at paragraph 7 says, specifically, "These people arrived without me being informed" and it also says, "These people were brought to us but I never had prior discussion with anyone from the hospital or the command of Zvornik Brigade regarding these wounded people." And so there is a distinction being drawn between when the order arrived versus when the people arrived. And I think that's probably the source of the confusion. I don't know if that satisfies my colleague. I can certainly put it to the witness if the Court needs further clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I would prefer if you put it to the witness rather than making a statement yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm just pointing out what's in the record, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest that having already told you that it needs some clarification, that you put the same problem --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- matter to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You have heard the concerns of the Court and also my colleague, Mr. Bourgon, concerning when it is that -- well, first of all, whether or not you received any prior notice as to the arrival of these wounded people. Could you just explain to the Court or tell the Court if that's, in fact, the case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't informed about any arrival of the wounded. They appeared all of a sudden, escorted by some soldiers. They appeared in the infirmary. Not all of them were brought in, some perhaps two or three. Then those who escorted them said these are the prisoners, the wounded, they're going to be exchanged in Bijeljina. So we took them out of that room where we were working. So I didn't understand because they brought them in and then they said these people are going to be exchanged in Bijeljina. Then after a couple of hours, we saw that these people had not been taken to exchange but were rather put in a place that was secured by military policemen. And then after that, Mr. Dragan Obrenovic came and told me what I told you earlier. I wasn't informed about any arrival of these people. I wasn't informed that they would come to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just so that the record is, I think, clear, are you saying essentially that you became aware of the presence of the wounded people before you saw Major Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are you also saying that you became aware of the written fax order after you saw Major Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. That was on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Is that -- is that satisfactory for my colleague?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon? Okay. Yes, he seems to be happy for once. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. You have indicated that these -- these individuals were brought to a specific area where you were working. First of all, let me just ask you, if you can recall, about what date that was.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to remember the date. I know it was July. It was summertime. As for the date, I don't know, and I don't know the day of the week either.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Fair to say you were working that day, right? You were on duty?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And you were in a specific area of the hospital, you've indicated. Could you just tell us where that was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: That wasn't the hospital, that was the barracks that had an infirmary. Well, how should I explain this? There are several entrances. So the first entrances when you enter the compound of the Standard factory, and then immediately to the right, some 20, 30 metres, was the infirmary and the kitchen was across from the infirmary. And then some 10 to 15 metres away from us were the premises of the military police and that one room where they stayed. So there was that portion of the compound. At the floor above, we had a clinic with some beds. And then there was a large bathroom between us and the police. I think that, to the right, as you entered, there was a large bathroom and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you indicated that they were brought in by a number of soldiers. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in relation to where they were taken, after they were brought to that room, did you have any discussion with anybody concerning where they should be placed or where they would be placed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: When Mr. Dragan Obrenovic came, then he started talking. He said that they would be accommodated there, that that was the safest place for them, that they would be secured by the military police and that was the only room where they could have been accommodated, but because everything else was full and I guess for their personal safety, it was a good idea to have police nearby. I guess that was the idea, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And so from the area where you worked, they were taken to another room; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... you to make any special accommodation, move things or make an arrangement in order to have those people placed in that room?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing was moved. There were pallets there, and then boards and then mattresses were placed on top of that. Soft mattresses. So it was a room of, I don't know the square footage of it. Normally, people who were trouble-makers in units were taken to that room. Either they were excessively drinking or abandoning their posts and normally they were brought to that room and military police was there to guard them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to these particular individuals, did you discuss with Major Obrenovic the circumstances as to how they would be secured or where they would be secured?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Most likely he had arranged that with the military police. What he told me was that they needed to be under strict care and observation in terms of their treatment: bandaging, dressing the wounds, giving them medication and so on. I was told to take very good care of them in the medical sense. As for their personal safety, I guess it was arranged with the military police. We received our instructions in writing on the following day about how to take care of the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you discuss with Major Obrenovic who would be taking care of the prisoners, whether it would be doctors from the Standard or doctors from the hospital, Zvornik Hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic told me on that same day, when he came to tell me that, that it had already been arranged, I guess, with the director of the Zvornik medical centre, about the surgeons who would be coming every day to treat the wounded. He said that they would only be treating those wounded, and not other wounded who were members of the army of Republika Srpska and who were only lightly wounded and who were staying at the clinic, which was on the floor above. But these surgeons from the hospital came exclusively to treat these wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you discuss with Major Obrenovic whether or not these wounded should be registered at the Standard?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On that same day, when Mr. Obrenovic came and said what he said, he also said that the surgeons from the Zvornik medical centre would be coming, so I told them -- told him that I would start medical charts for them, with their daily body temperature taken and so on, their diagnosis would be entered into that chart and so on. And then I asked Mr. Obrenovic whether I should also register them in the logbook, and he said no, that wasn't necessary, just those charts would be sufficient. Then I proposed to Mr. Obrenovic, and he agreed, that once these people are taken to be exchanged to Bijeljina, then these medical charts should accompany them, so that the doctors who received them at the other end, after the exchange, would know exactly what kind of treatment they had received because it would make their job easier, and Mr. Obrenovic agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the creation of these charts, did you -- did you do that with respect to each one of the wounded?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: We started these medical charts or temperature charts for each of the wounded and we kept it in a file. We typically had this for all members of the Zvornik Brigade who were wounded. In the morning, when doctors were doing their morning rounds, they would look at the chart and, you know, decide whether the wound needed to be dressed again, what kind of treatment they needed to receive on that day, and then the chart would be put back into the file until the following day. And the rules were such that we made rounds several times during the day, provide water, cigarettes, whatever we could give them we did. And as for treating the wounds, it was done by surgeons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the charts that you created, they contained typical medical information, such as the temperature of the patient, blood pressure, medication, age, date of birth, and name of the patient. Is that -- is that basically what information they contained?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to the treatment that the wounded actually received, you have indicated that that was administered by doctors or surgeons from the Zvornik Hospital. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect to the entries that they made on these medical charts, did that involve your staff in any way? Did they have to go to your staff in order to get access to those charts?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. As soon as the surgeon would appear in the morning, a nurse would take out charts, that was the rule. So she would take out these charts with temperatures and all other information, hand them to the surgeon, and the surgeon would call them in one by one, check their wounds, dress them, prescribe further therapy and then the next patient would come in. I can't remember when they typically came, but I think it was early, at about 8.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you have occasion to -- to yourself look at some of these medical charts from time to time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. It was all on a table. And naturally we commented upon them with surgeons. I personally was interested in surgery, so I followed closely what surgeons did. So there were some parameters on that chart, diagnosis, bandages, that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court in general the type of condition these wounded were in when you received them at the Standard?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: As for the types of wounds, those were not life-threatening wounds. Normally those were wounds created by shrapnels on lower extremities. What I remember is that one of them did not have an arm below his elbow, and the other one did not have a leg before the knee. They were properly treated. I remember the man without the leg. I remember his last name. I don't remember his first name but I remember his last name because it was the same as mine, Begovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect to that individual, you have indicated that he had a -- that he was without a leg. Was that the result of -- did it appear to you that that was the result of an amputation or some kind of treatment in relation to an injury?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. An amputation was done, and one could see that it was properly sutured. The amputation was done.
