I don't know whether it was done in Zvornik or elsewhere, but that's how he was brought to us. He had bandages on his leg, he did not have anything below his knee. And as for the other wounded, mostly shrapnels, shrapnel wounds on their legs, some of them had stomach injuries but none of them had life-threatening wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You have indicated also that at some point you became aware that the wounded had been removed from the centre. And just to get an idea in terms of time, can you approximate when this was in relation to when they arrived? How many days?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: You mean how many days they spent with us? Well, they were there between five to seven days, as is stated there. I can't remember whether it was five or seven, but it was approximately that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, following their removal, can you tell us whether or not the medical charts that you created went with them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, the medical charts stayed with the rest of the patient files where the files of the soldiers of the Zvornik Brigade were kept. The lists were not sent off with them, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect to the medical papers -- well, let me rephrase that. Did you see that they arrived with medical papers from any -- any other place, any other hospital or any other facility?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: I can recall that when they were brought, first they were in Milici, then in Zvornik, then they were brought to us. And from what I can remember, they had discharge papers. I don't know whether it was from the Zvornik Hospital; there was also a hospital in Milici. They had these small discharge papers and those papers were placed together with the temperature charts. So based on those discharge papers, I was copying the diagnosis from them into the temperature charts. And all of that was put together in a list that was supposed to go with them when they went off for exchange. There was supposed to be a medical escort also to go with them, but nobody informed us that they were leaving, so the documents stayed in a file together with the rest of the medical files.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when you say a medical escort, could you just tell us what you mean by that? Do you mean a doctor or a technician or...

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: It was our custom and rule that the wounded who were sent to the Zvornik medical centre would, along with the driver, be also escorted by a medical technician. No patient could go to the medical centre who had been with us at the infirmary, who had been admitted to the infirmary, could not go to the medical centre without a -- an ambulance and a medical escort. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, you've -- you've indicated that part of what wasn't included in your statement referred to some other individuals that were brought to the Standard. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. You mean after the group, were others brought in? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's my question. Is that what you had indicated wasn't in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that. The group, when they were taken away, we were not told where, but from the first day it was known that they were going to Bijeljina for an exchange. So I don't know whether a day or two or three days later, when we were working at the clinic, the door opened suddenly and a man was brought in on a stretcher. He was carried in by four people, and the fifth one was lying on the stretcher. They were all Muslims, they were accompanied by a policeman or a soldier, I can't remember which, and he was wounded in the belly. And I lifted his shirt, he was wounded in the belly, and I cleaned the wound and I said that this person has to go to Zvornik urgently, a surgeon needs to look at him because I couldn't see how deep the wound was. But the people who brought him in said, well, the bus is waiting, they urgently have to go to Bijeljina for the exchange. So they lifted him up and I mean it didn't take long, the whole thing took maybe some 10 minutes or so, not more than that. This was after that group -- so this group and the previous group had nothing to do with each other. The other people were admitted, they were treated and then they went for the exchange. I can't remember about this other group, they just came in, I looked at the wound and they left very quickly because they said the transport was waiting for them. The gentleman who questioned me three years ago, I think I heard from him that those people had been exchanged. I didn't know what their fate was and that was the first time I heard about that. Three years ago, he asked if I knew anything about them, and I said, I didn't. And then he said that those people had been exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Just so that we can clarify this a little bit on the record, with respect to the first group and the second group, could you tell us approximately how many individuals were involved in this first group of people that were admitted and treated, et cetera? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Between 10 and 14, perhaps 10, perhaps 14, perhaps 12. That's about the size of the group approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In relation to the second group, can you tell us approximately how many individuals were involved in relation to that incident?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: This other group I think that they were five. Four people brought in, they were carrying the stretcher, and there was the first person lying on the stretcher. So five.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the second group, those individuals you indicated were not admitted, weren't -- they weren't kept at the Standard for any length of time, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: They came in suddenly. The person was lying on the stretcher. We don't know who he was. We could see they were Muslims. He was wounded in the belly. The wound was dressed and he was given an IV. I didn't know if any abdominal organs were damaged, so I told the person who was escorting him that the person should be taken to the Zvornik Hospital, so the surgeon can look at him. However, he said, transport is waiting for them, they have to go to Bijeljina urgently, so they just picked him up and that was it. It didn't take that long; 10 minutes at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So for this second group, did you create any charts or records in relation to them containing their names and medical information?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't make any charts or anything. It was very sudden, very fast, and I dressed the wound. I put the IV in and then they just left. We didn't take their first names or their last names. This is all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, even though you didn't take the names, were you ever provided with their names by anybody in relation to either their arrival or at some point after?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Doctor. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. I've got several Defence teams wishing to cross-examine you, Dr. Begovic, with the exception of the Borovcanin Defence team which still needs to be confirmed. Who wishes to go first? Mr. Zivanovic for Accused Popovic. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to tell me a couple of things relating to the statement that you gave, this was on the 2nd of April, 2003. You said that you were summoned by a policeman, that he brought the summons?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was this summons in our language? We call it here our language the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was on a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I suggest you slow down immediately, and I think on previous occasions you had chosen to keep the headphones on so that you could have an indication when the English interpretation was over, and that helped a lot in keeping the momentum as it should be. So, Witness, if possible, please, Dr. Begovic, if possible, please allow a short pause between question and answer so that the interpreters can carry out their job and finish translating to us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: These summons that are delivered by our authorities, they contain a warning that you have to comply and turn up, otherwise you could be fined or detained. Is that what the -- what was said in the summons too?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And I was surprised when the summons was delivered. It was written on the back, but also he told me too that I had to comply with the summons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And when you did comply, did you understand that -- that you had to comply, not only to come, but that you also had to provide a statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know what would happen. I didn't know that a statement would be involved. There was simply said that an investigator from the Tribunal is coming, he needs to see something with you and you should turn up at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you told that you can provide a statement, but that you do not have to or did you understand that you were obliged to provide a statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't told that. Simply the gentleman and the interpreter were waiting for me in the room and the interview began.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say this wasn't told to you, what you mean is that you were not told that you had to give a statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have the date when the statement was taken, that's the 2nd of April, 2003. I would like to ask you to tell me how long did the interview last with the investigator?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: I can't really tell you how long it took. It was for an hour and a half or two for sure. I really cannot say how long it took, but that was it, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, after speaking with the investigator, there was a written statement in English that was drafted?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask to read it in your own language?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I did not. The lady that was interpreting said, I'm now going to read back to you what you stated. And then as soon as she started to read, I told her to stop and then I complained because it said there that I had come voluntarily, but I had actually been summoned. So that's when we stopped, because I didn't come voluntarily. I had received a summons, but the gentleman said that was it. But that wasn't it. I had received a summons and this was not corrected. And I saw that here when I read it back two days ago. Also, in several places, as she was reading, I would stop the lady and make suggestions, but it stayed the way it was. I mean, look, I apologise, I explained to the gentleman that this other group was there too, which is very important, and a wounded man was brought in. It's not there anywhere. After this other group, it wasn't put in the statement. The gentleman asked, What about Mr. Pandurevic? In the statement it says, I think that Mr. Pandurevic did not visit the wounded. Well, he didn't because he wasn't there. I told him that. And this wasn't taken down. Why was it not taken down that Mr. Pandurevic wasn't there, I asked him. I saw Mr. Pandurevic the first time after all that happened was already done. The way it looks in the statement is that Mr. Pandurevic was there, but he didn't visit them. But he wasn't actually there, and I said in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So from this answer of yours, I can conclude that you had several objections or remarks regarding the statement the way it was read back to you but this was not taken into account?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: I said the same things two days ago, and I thought that that would be corrected on the basis of my remarks. I thought that that would be corrected, but I see it's the same as it was two days ago. But I signed it, yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like you to tell me, were you given any reasons why they would not take into account the corrections?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: This is right at the end. When it was read to me, it was signed, it was read back, and I told the lady who was translating about that and I saw that she asked him. I don't speak English, but I could see that she talked to him. Then, also at that time, I indicated at several places, I mean immediately when she started to read, immediately at the start, I didn't come there voluntarily. I had come because of the summons and that was not corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, the interpreter conveyed to the investigator your remarks?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. That is correct. I really didn't -- I really thought...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to be in the interpreter's shoes. You are moving too fast. Please slow down. It's a matter of courtesy for the interpreters who already have a very difficult job, and on whom we need to rely. So please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And just one more question on this topic. You did not receive any answer from the investigator regarding your remarks?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So since then, since the 6th of April, 2003, until a few days ago when you arrived here, were you in contact with the investigators of the Tribunal in that period?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to ask you about this other group of detainees that arrived, about which you said that they didn't stay long at the infirmary or the clinic. Can you tell us approximately how much time elapsed from when the first group left until the second group arrived?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: A day or two. I cannot really remember exactly, but I think it was within a day or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And just one more question. It has to do with putting information in about the first group of patients. You said that Obrenovic told you not to register these patients in your logbooks.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: I asked Obrenovic if we should put them in the logbooks and he said the lists are sufficient and that was it. And when I told him that we would be sending the lists together with them, the charts, at the exchange, so that the doctors there can see how they were treated and what sort of treatment they were administered, Mr. Obrenovic disagreed and he said that that was sufficient, that we shouldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: After this group left, were you in touch with Mr. Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: I would see very little of Mr. Obrenovic. I saw him that day when the order was conveyed to us, and then I didn't see him for a long time. He was absent out in the field. There were very few of us at the barracks at the time. I would see him, but very infrequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is, after the group left, did you have the opportunity of seeing him at all?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: I did see him, but I don't know exactly when. You mean did I see him the next day?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm just asking in general, did you see him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would see him, but I don't know how much time had elapsed since they left when I saw him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You started moving fast again. Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My last question is, did you speak with him when you saw him afterwards? Did you talk at all about this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You did not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the witness had already answered the question and I was going to object as asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Who wishes to go next? Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For General Beara. You requested 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Begovic. How are you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. How are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I was just waiting for the answer to be given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next we'll have the exchange of bouquets of flowers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: During your meeting with the Prosecution and their investigators, did they ever show you the Zvornik Brigade duty officer logbook?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... also, sir, during any of the meetings that you had with the Prosecution or any of their investigators, did they show you any intercepts?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you just help me, if you remember, back in 1995, whether there were any people where you worked who had the name of Ljubo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: There was a dentist Ljubo Dzeric. I actually replaced him. I came and he was demobilised sometime in June 1994. He was the chief of the medical service before I arrived. That's the Ljubo that I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And his first name is Ljubomir, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Ljubomir, yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were there any other individuals, to the best of your recollection, who were in Zvornik at that time who went by the name of Ljubo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would object to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On what basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On the grounds that it's not -- I don't think it's properly circumscribed. Zvornik is a pretty big area and I think that the question is unfairly put to the witness and I wonder if my colleague can be more precise if he's referring to a given location, group or entity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he can answer that question. Let's let him answer it. He's perfectly capable of answering, given what the question is and how vague it is. Can you repeat your question, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will. And I'll try to make not as vague.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, in July of 1995, in the Zvornik area where you were, during the time that you were there, do you remember any other military people with the name -- going by the first name Ljubo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... thank you, doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Who wishes to go next? Mr. Bourgon for Nikolic. You requested 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: A few questions for you today. The first one being, the officer within the headquarters who was responsible for the infirmary, I mean the officer you responded to, would I be correct in saying that that was Sreten Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Sreten Milosevic was the logistics commander and my first ranking superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I read from your statement now, Doctor, and I see that your immediate supervisor was Lieutenant Nikolic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was Lieutenant Nikolic, but very soon, when I came to the barracks in 1994, he was replaced, I think, by Sreten Milosevic. It was sometime in 1994 when I came. I don't know whether it was in early 1995 or late 1994, when Bosko Nikolic was replaced by Sreten Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, of course, as you -- my question was exactly that, that the Lieutenant Nikolic we're talking about, that is not Drago Nikolic. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Not Drago Nikolic, but Bosko Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my next question deals with the fact that these persons that were detained, we're talking about those Muslims and I refer now to the transcript, and that was on page 42, starting at line 21. And you say that this wasn't the hospital, that was the barracks that had an infirmary. And I'll just quote you from the transcript here, "Why should I explain this? There are several entrances, so the first entrance is when you enter the compound of the Standard factory, then immediately to the right, some 20 to 30 metres was the infirmary. The kitchen was across from the infirmary. And then 10 to 15 metres away from us was the premises of the military police and that one room where they stayed." Now, my question to you is, these Muslim prisoners, they were in the care and custody at that time of the military police. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the detention room where people, trouble-makers from units were usually kept. That was that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my next question is, they, according to your testimony, stayed at the barracks there from five to seven days, and during which -- during which they were treated by the surgeons from the hospital, and you did those temperature charts. Now -- and you also described a bit what kind of -- what kind of -- in what medical conditions they were. My question is simple: These persons, when they were taken away from the Standard barracks, were they fit to travel?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. Nobody was in life-threatening condition and they were fit to travel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Bourgon. Who wishes to go next? I have the Miletic, the Gvero and the Pandurevic teams left. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We won't have any questions for this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. And that was for General Miletic. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The position is the same for General Gvero, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Josse. So that leaves you, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Begovic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You have mentioned that during the time you were working at the Standard barracks your immediate commander was latterly Sreten Milosevic, and initially Bosko Nikolic. Were they the only two commanders you had during the time that you were at Standard?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Sreten Milosevic was replaced by Major Jojic. That's how it was. He stayed there very briefly. I think that was in late 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. So in the course of about 18 months, you had three different commanding officers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was that typical of the sort of turnover of command staff in the Zvornik Brigade during that period?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it was typical. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not sure whether you've actually covered this, but we'll go into it anyway. The facilities at the infirmary were perfectly adequate for looking after the sort of wounded people that you had there for that five or seven days, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was an infirmary consisting of two rooms. We also had the portion where the wounded members of the army of Republika Srpska were in beds and that was up on the floor, and it was completely full.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you have permanent staff available to care for these people?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: This was permanent staff. It's just that they worked in shifts. They went home and the others came, but there was always somebody there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just give us some idea. When you say there was always somebody there, was there always a doctor there and always nursing staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: There was always a doctor, always nurses, medical technicians. When there was no combat, then male staff members would be there as well, and when there was active combat, then there would be only female staff there. There would always be a doctor, since we had three male doctors and three female doctors, and there would always be nurses and there were always two on each shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the doctors that visited from the Zvornik Hospital, did they come every morning during the time that the prisoners you've talked about were there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Every morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you tell us this: How far is it from the Standard barracks at Karakaj to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Zvornik-Bijeljina is 56 kilometres, which means that there is about 53 kilometres, thereabout, because Zvornik-Karakaj is two or three kilometres, so I would say 53 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how long would it take to transport people that sort of distance?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: About an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. So can we summarise the position as you understood it. You were not expecting these prisoners to arrive; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: They arrived with discharge certificates from other hospitals; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: They were registered and records were kept by you as to their treatment throughout the whole time they were there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Records were kept by the surgeon who came, so the surgeon would take the chart and the surgeon would look at the previous treatment prescribed by another surgeon, you know, add, subtract, and we would simply check that if we needed to assist with anything. However, these wounded were in the exclusive care of surgeons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to repeat, they were adequately cared for by you and visited every day by staff from the hospital. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And your expectation was that they were going to be transported to Batkovci which is in Bijeljina together with their records; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: In Bijeljina, not in Batkovac. That's how it was stated originally. Mr. Obrenovic said what I have already told you that they were going to be exchanged in Bijeljina. I proposed to Obrenovic and he agreed that when they set out to go for the exchange, their temperature charts should accompany them so that the doctors on the other end, who took them over would have an easier job. Mr. Obrenovic supported this and that's where we left it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, just one thing whilst we're on the subject of Mr. Obrenovic. You have talked about a fax that you saw and the content of that fax. Were you able to see from the fax who it was sent by?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether the fax arrived from the Main Staff or from the corps. I don't know. To this day I don't know that. I'm not sure whether it arrived from the Main Staff or from the corps. And I don't know whether it was signed by Mr. Mladic or somebody else. I had the fax with the order, but to tell you the truth, I don't know whether it came from the medical -- from the corps or from the Main Staff. But it was in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So was it the content of that fax that gave you some idea as to where it came from, if you don't know who it was from?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't be able to say, because faxes are generally similar except for the signature. Roughly it was similar to what Mr. Obrenovic said. Whatever Mr. Obrenovic said was written in the fax, but I don't know who wrote it, I don't know if it came from the corps or the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So the position is this: You saw a fax which made it plain that prisoners were to be exchanged and Major Obrenovic who was then in command of the brigade told you that these prisoners were to be exchanged. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Mr. Obrenovic said on the day before, what you just repeated. And then on the following day it arrived in writing. Again, I don't know whether it came from the Main Staff or the corps. But whatever Mr. Obrenovic said, it was said the day before the order which arrived by fax.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did Mr. Obrenovic ever say anything to you about seeking guidance from the corps or the Main Staff as to what was to be done with wounded prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: No. He said it to me the day before it arrived in writing. And that's where it ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I just want to move on now, please, to the second group that you referred to, the group of five. Were you at the infirmary the day that that group arrived?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was there, and another lady doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were the doctors at the infirmary at that point in time. The lady doctor's name is Danijela Lazic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Now, so far as that group of five were concerned, were you aware whether any two of them were brothers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you aware whether any of that group of five left to go to hospital and have an X-ray?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you aware whether that group of five were given food?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: We had some bread there and we gave them cigarettes. I remember that I had three or four packs of cigarettes. Since I am not a smoker myself, I gave this to this young patient who was 20 something. I gave all three or four packs to him and then we had some bread there and we gave it to them. That's all we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And is it your recollection that this group was there as long as three hours, or not that long?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: I know that they were at our infirmary for some 10 minutes, perhaps more, perhaps less. The one who was on the stretchers was the only one who was wounded. He was lying on the stretcher. His wound was dressed, cleaned. He was given IV fluids. Then I said that the man who was wounded had to be sent to Zvornik to be seen by a surgeon. However, the person escorting them said they were in a hurry, there is a transportation awaiting them to take them to Bijeljina. There was no time to do that, and then they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Doctor. I just wonder whether we could have in e-court, please, 7D257. I apologise in advance, this is not a document that has yet been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. While we're waiting for that, could I ask the Court could we stay briefly after the break, after the witness leaves. There is a matter I need to bring up just briefly; I just remembered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Is it in relation to the motion that you have just filed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to raise it up myself anyway. Yes, I apologise to you, Mr. Haynes, for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm going to need your help now. This is a document which is only in Serbian. I'm going direct you to a passage of it and I would like you to read it out loud slowly so that the interpreters can interpret it into English and French for us. Do you understand? Do you understand what I'd like you to do?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. Well, what I'm going to do in a minute is I'm going to have the usher bring this document up to a passage I would like you to read. But I'd like you to read it out loud slowly so that the interpreters can translate it into English and French for us. Do you understand that? Could we bring the document --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: I see right now or...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, I'll take you to the passage. Can it come up a little bit? Can you go -- count up from the bottom, I think about 10 lines, and can you see the sentence that begins, "Doveli su"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it's two lines above that that's where you should go. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's actually underlined the starting line. And it -- it's about three quarters of the way along. The cursor is in the right place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Doctor, would you mind just reading from there to the bottom of the page at quite a gentle pace, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. "They brought them to the administration building of engineering that -- which was a construction company."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think you can read a little faster than that, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: All right. "They took them into some corridor. They searched them there. They took from them shoelaces, belts, and took them to the boiler room, 11 of them. The two brothers were separated; they were wounded. (They were wounded before they were arrested), one of the brothers was called Hasan, they were from Osat. Later an investigator came and policemen (they had white cross-belts and belts), and they gave their personal details one by one. They did not mistreat them. They brought another 11 people from Srebrenica, and they gave them food. They told them that the two who were wounded went to see a doctor and that they should leave some food for them. They didn't take them -- they didn't bring them to the boiler room. And after three hours they took out prisoners who were tied. And next to a truck (a truck of the former JNA with tarpaulin) they saw the two wounded brothers. They were holding X-ray pictures. They had seen the doctor. They took all of them to Batkovici with two police cars escorting them."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your help, Doctor. Just two or three things about that. The -- the "Inzinjering," can you see that word. I can't say it very well, but it's on the far left-hand side, nine lines up. Go to the left, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's an area -- that's an area at the Standard barracks at Karakaj, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: No. Inzinjering is a different company. It's not the same company as Standard. It's a company that is further. Once you pass Karakaj, you pass the Standard barracks and then some 300 or 400 metres later you come to an overpass and then I think on the left is this company called Inzinjering. Inzinjering and Standard are not the same companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, but the Inzinjering was never used as a military facility, was it, in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. Standard was used. The shoe factory, which existed before the war. It was used as the barracks. As for Inzinjering, I don't think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And the only other thing is if you just read out to yourself, we're talking here about a group of people who arrived at Batkovci on the 24th of July, aren't we, if you look further up the paragraph? Can you see on the letter there is a date that is circled?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: It says the 24th of July, 1995, at about 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, the group that are described there with the two wounded brothers, one of whom is called Hasan and who went off to get an X-ray at hospital, that's not the same group of five you're talking about, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: The one who was brought to the infirmary in the second group that came did not have any X-rays on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you've already told us you weren't aware of any two of them being brothers or going off to hospital.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And they certainly weren't there for three hours or so. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: I told you they were there between five and 10 minutes. It all happened very quickly. All I managed to do was to clean and dress the wound and give him IV fluids. That's all I had the time to do, not more than 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I just want to finish with one last thing. Before you met an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor, your belief was that these 11 people who had been in your care at the infirmary had all been sent to Bijeljina for exchange.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in the years, in the 10 years between those events and when you met an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor, you heard nothing from any source that caused you to think anything other than that, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BEGOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. I heard of them for the first time, the first group, and the second group, when the gentleman interviewed me three years ago. I truly didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Haynes. Is there re-examination? Yes, Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correction for the transcript in two places, please. Page 66, line 20. The witness mentioned the name of the doctor or, rather, the last name of the lady doctor, who was present with him. So could we ask the witness to repeat that last name? And then on page 70, line 24, the date was wrongly recorded as the 14th of July and it should be the 24th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I can confirm that last one because I had noticed it myself, but I didn't want to interrupt the witness. As regards the other one, did you mention the name of the lady doctor who was with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Danijela Lazic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sarapa and thank you, Dr. Begovic. Is there re-examination, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, there's not, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dr. Begovic, your testimony ends here. We haven't got any questions for you. So you're free to go. You will receive all the assistance you require from the staff of our Tribunal. On behalf of which I would like to thank you for having come over here to give evidence, and I also, on behalf of everyone, wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go into private session for -- I mean, we'll come to the exhibits later, but let's -- in the few minutes that we have, deal with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will now have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's process with the exhibits first. Exhibits first, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have only the witness statement, P02481, to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections? We hear none. So admitted. Defence teams, I think it was only the Pandurevic Defence team that made use of a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, it's untranslated. It's 7D257. It's a report of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Presidency state commission for gathering facts on war crimes. Can it be marked for identification at this stage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Haynes. Any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have no objection to having it marked for identification, but I would like to see a translation of it and perhaps reserve an objection to that extent if it is otherwise objectionable. I can't tell from either the testimony or what I was able to see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not the normal practice that we resort to. It will be marked for identification purposes pending translation. And after which it will come into the record as an exhibit. I mean, if you have any objections in relation to the admission proper, speak now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's just a bit difficult for me to articulate because I don't know if it contains otherwise objectionable matter other than what was referred to in the testimony. And I think the document covers more material than what the witness was specifically directed to. That's the only reason why I would ask to -- ask you to consider allowing me to reserve the objection until I see the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm just going to say this: It comes from the EDS, it's a Prosecution document. We served due notice that we were going to use it in cross-examination. They should be able, with all the interpreters and army of helpers they've got at their disposal, to voice an objection now if they've got one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How many pages does that document contain?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Page and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page and a half. And we've seen half of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't want to blow this up, but the usual practice that we have followed here is to mark it for identification pending translation and then it will become a full exhibit. On the other hand -- even if one were to entertain objections here, and entertain objections against the admission of the document, et cetera, part of it or the -- the part which was of relevance to Mr. Haynes was read out and it's in the record already.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have no problem with that. My only concern was with respect to extraneous material. I'm perfectly fine following the process. If I discover that there's something egregious in the document later, I'll bring it to the attention of the Court. At this point, I will withdraw the objection and proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's admitted on that condition, marked for identification pending translation. Gentlemen and ladies, can I come back to you on the two pending motions, one oral, one written, seeking protective measures for the next two witnesses. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think we've all basically met and discussed it and conferred with our learned friends at the Prosecution. We don't really see that the rules have been followed specifically, especially at the late stage, but we do not have an objection to that request, if the witnesses feel there is some need and we would defer to your better judgement on that, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We want to know whether there is any objection from any one of the other Defence teams. You seem to be speaking on behalf of everyone. So we take it that there is no objection. Just one moment. I need to confer again with my colleagues with whom I have discussed already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So our decision is as follows, and we are deciding both motions, that relating to the next witness who is Witness 152, and the other relating to Witness 155, the latter of which is the subject matter of the written motion. We have opted to go on an abundance of caution approach, particularly basing ourselves on the fact that both parties are in agreement that granting of protective measures in these two cases could be appropriate, or may be appropriate. We would also, however, like to make it clear that we are not saying anything beyond this. In particular, we don't want this decision to serve later on as a precedent for granting protective measures to others who may have similar or identical conditions. So the protective measures are a pseudonym and -- pseudonym and face distortion. Even for the first witness that we are going to hear for the first one, the one who will be entering the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would apply for it. But I would leave it really in your discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm asking you because since this is -- has not been incorporated in a written document, Mr. McCloskey referred to -- and you, to protective measures, but not identifying any. I mean, we take it that pseudonym is -- is usual, normal. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Pseudonym and face distortion. We just -- because of the problems related to voice, and given the history, I wouldn't ask for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So both motions are granted and I wish to thank the members of the various Defence teams for their cooperation. Thank you. While we are waiting for the witness, you may have heard in the course of last week and this week that there was an anticipated strike, transport strike for Friday, this Friday. We've just received a confirmation that although the strike is still on it will not affect the transfer of our detainees to and from the Tribunal. Therefore, the scheduled trials for Friday will go ahead as planned. So if anyone was planning to stay working at home or in the office on Friday, now you need to forget all about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence, which will take some time. Before you start, you need to make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. Madam Registrar is giving you the text of it. Please read it out aloud and that will be your commitment with us that you will testify the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. Take a seat. I'll be only a minute. Mr. Vanderpuye, who you have met already, will go first. He will be referring you to statements and will also ask you a few questions. He will then be followed by various of the Defence teams on cross-examination. I do not anticipate your testimony to finish today, possibly also not tomorrow. You might still be here afterwards, until Monday. So, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you just bear with me for one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, before you continue, because -- just before you entered the courtroom, that's about an hour ago, not just before, the Prosecution asked for your behalf to have in place some protective measures. And that's for reasons that you explained to the Prosecution and which the Prosecution explained to us in turn. We consulted with the various Defence teams, and the various Defence teams also agreed with the Prosecution that it would be appropriate to have two protective measures in place. One is the use of a pseudonym instead of your name, and that's why I didn't address you by your name when you entered the courtroom. The second is we are going to hide your visual appearance. There will be a facial -- what we call a facial distortion. I trust this has been explained to you and that it is to your satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am satisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Back to you, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm going to hand a document, P02484, for the record. Please take a look at that and can you just confirm that you are the person named on it without reading it out loud?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to put to you some questions, but before I do, I just wanted to point out a couple of things. As the President has indicated, you are the beneficiary of certain protective measures. And in my questions to you, I will try to be as mindful of that as I can, and I will try to avoid mentioning anything that may tend to reveal your identity. And I would ask that, first, you try to do the same thing. Second, that when you -- before answering a question, you allow a short pause so that the translators can translate what's been said into the various languages. And that you wait until the end of the question before you commence your answer, and ask if there is anything that's unclear about the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Before you proceed. And just in case Mr. Vanderpuye, since we are not privy to what the testimony -- what the witness will -- the details of the witness's testimony, I'm leaving it entirely in your discretion to inform us in good time if we need to have recourse to Rule 90(E). I don't know. You should be in a much better position than the Trial Chamber. But if it's the case, please come back to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can we go into private session? I would like to go into basic background of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us where you were born?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162
utterances.text: I was born in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And where were you raised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162
utterances.text: In Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you attend school there, work there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162
utterances.text: I completed elementary school in Bratunac and secondary school in Bijeljina, and first level of college in -- in Tuzla. And I worked for my whole life in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, at some point in your career you became active in politics, in local, municipal politics. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And could you tell us briefly what positions you held in municipal politics?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162
utterances.text: I held several positions in municipal politics during wartime and also before the war. Before the war I was in the League of Communists and I had positions there. I was a member of the municipal committee in Bratunac. I was a councilman in the municipal assembly. I also was the vice-president of the municipal council of Bratunac. All of this was before the war. When war broke out I -- well, before the war, I worked at the local police as well for one term of office, as deputy chief of the Bratunac police. This was from 1980 to 1984. After that I was appointed as director of the people's university in Bratunac, and I worked there until the beginning of the war. That's what -- that was my job when the work -- when the war broke out in 1991. From October 1994 on, I worked as president of the Bratunac municipality Executive Board. I was appointed to that work by Bratunac municipal assembly and I worked there until March 1997, when I came back and was the director of the Bratunac cultural centre. This is a brief overview of my political and other jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. In 1995, if I could just direct your attention to July of that year. You held the position in Bratunac as president of the Executive Board at that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us briefly what your responsibilities were in that position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162
utterances.text: The Executive Board is a body that is like a government. I was at the head of that local government. That is the sort of description of what an Executive Board is. Should I also say what the duties of the Executive Board were at that time? At the time, the Executive Board was - if I can just collect myself for a minute - logistics brigade to the Bratunac Brigade, at the time that was our number one task. Then in relation to the population, to provide utilities to the citizens and to the town to make sure the town had water, electricity, that the schools were working, the health institutions were working, that the town was properly supplied with food, articles, that the shops were working. Because in Bratunac itself, there were no combat actions, only around Bratunac. So that would be in brief what the duties of the Executive Board were in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. If I could, I'd like to draw your attention specifically to the 11th of July of that year, of 1995. Do you recall that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And could you tell us basically what you recall specifically about that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162
utterances.text: I remember that that day I went to a village of Pribicevac, which is about 20 kilometres from Bratunac. The 3rd Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade was accommodated in that village, and in this 3rd Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade was where my son was, who was in charge of the battalion logistics. I went to Pribicevac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. We are in private session, all right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I was just going to ask if we could go to open session from this point forward. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But please, Witness, look at me. We are going into open session now. And you need to avoid saying things which could identify you. Just now, for example, you stated what position your son held and where. That could go as a means of identifying you. So don't mention names associated with you that could identify you or events with which you are associated in a way that could identify you. All right? Okay. Let's go into open session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I believe you were -- you were talking about having gone to Pribicevac. Could you tell the Court -- could you tell the Court why it is that you went there and if it calls for -- well, if it calls for a name, just avoid mentioning any names.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162
utterances.text: I went to visit the 3rd Battalion and to see what was going on there. And I stopped by this logistics unit and I stayed there with the people I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did you go there alone or did you go with somebody? And...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162
utterances.text: There was another man with me from the brigade, a friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can we just go into private session to identify this person?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means, let's go into private session

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us who the person is now that you went to Pribicevac with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162
utterances.text: Assistant commander for logistics was with me. He cooperated closely with the Executive Board when it came to logistics for the brigade, so we went there together in order to see what the situation was with the army when it came to uniforms, footwear, cigarettes, food, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, we are still in private session, so I would ask if you could just name the person for the record so the Court knows who we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162
utterances.text: Dragoslav Drisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We can go to open session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's revert to open session, please

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us about what time of day that occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162
utterances.text: It would have been in the morning, about 10 or 11.00. 10.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to discuss with this person the genesis, the reason why you were going there before you actually embarked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162
utterances.text: You mean with the person I went there with? Is that the person you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162
utterances.text: Yes, our goal was to see whether they needed anything in the 3rd Battalion in terms of clothes, footwear, food, cigarettes. The kitchen was up there. We wanted to see how it was operated, whether they had enough of everything, whether the troops were satisfied. That was the purpose of our visit there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you tell us, while you were there, you've mentioned that you did go there to see someone. Did you see anybody else while you were there that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162
utterances.text: In the house where the logistics was billeted, I stayed there with a person who was close to me and we sat there in the house. As for the friend who had arrived there with me, he went to the command post, which was some 200 to 300 metres further away. As I sat there in the house and talked with this close person, a vehicle stopped in front of the house. General Mladic came out of it. General Zivanovic was with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did you at any point have any contact with either General?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162
utterances.text: When the vehicle stopped in front of the house and when the soldiers started saying, "Here's the General, here's his vehicle," it was the Puch, everybody dispersed. And it was only the people who were in that logistics unit who remained there. I came out of the house into the yard. General's vehicle was some 30 metres away from the house. It couldn't come any closer because there was a truck parked in front of the house, a military truck, and they were loading ammunition or some military equipment on to the truck. Thus the General couldn't come closer with his vehicle, so he started cursing and yelling, saying, "Who parked this vehicle here?" He was saying all this on the go, as he was moving about. And in doing so, he came close to me. I stood there and he yelled at me, "Who are you? What are you doing here?" I introduced myself and he said angrily, "Get out of here." You know, "Go to the command post." I felt uncomfortable because I had come there in civilian clothes without weapons. Knowing the General, I was worried that he would criticise me for coming there without weapons or anything. So I figured that I should go into that house, grab somebody's rifle, and then go to the command post, as he told me. So I went in, found somebody's rifle, I don't know whose it was, I took it and then I was about to leave the house with it when I again came across the General at the door. He started yelling at me, saying, "Are you still here?" I just kept quiet, ran outside, and then moved away. As I was walking towards the command post *I came across Miroslav Deronjic, president of the municipal board of the SDS and Miodrag Josipovic, chief of police in Bratunac. I asked them how come you're here? And they said, We're running away from the General. He's yelling at everyone. I told them about the unpleasant encounter that I had just had with him and then we sat down in that spot from which we could see the house where the logistics support was. When we saw that the General moved away with his vehicle, I went back to the house. I said good-bye to this close person. My friend joined me by that time and then we got into the car that we had arrived there in originally and went back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, reading through page 89 through lines 7 to 9, at least two persons, namely Miroslav Deronjic, if he happens to be following the proceedings or to read this transcript, and Miodrag Josipovic, if he is still alive and is following or may read, who would immediately recognise who the witness is. I don't know if you wish to redact or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think out of an abundance of caution we can -- we can move to redact. I'll try to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'll try to direct the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's redact the names of those two individuals. Redact not only the names, but also their position at the time. Delete the next two -- all the words for the next two lines after the words, "I came across," the end of line 7 on page 89. Okay. Let's revert to open session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We are in open session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You had made a number of references previously to a General, just -- just now as you have been testifying. And you had indicated previous to that that you had contact -- well, that General Mladic was together with General Zivanovic. And with respect to the General that you have been speaking about having had an interaction with, which General is that, so that it's clear for the record?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162
utterances.text: You mean my unpleasant encounter?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I mean your unpleasant encounter.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162
utterances.text: General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you indicated that you encountered two individuals who you described previously. Did you encounter any -- any other person that you knew before you left for the day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162
utterances.text: Where do you mean? That I met them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm asking if you met anyone else in and around the vicinity of the command when you were in that area after having met the two people that you've just described in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162
utterances.text: That was at Pribicevac. That wasn't at the command post, no. That was out in the field, 20 kilometres from Bratunac. This is where the 3rd Battalion was billeted. I didn't meet anybody else there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162
utterances.text: Because this is out in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for just a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It will be just a moment because we are due to adjourn in about a minute's time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This would be actually the point then to break if it's all right with the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we will go back to open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I said, are you finishing this or are we breaking?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think it would be a good time to break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I thought. So let's go into open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's time and we stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.
